verses.t: Wan Zhang asked, "When Shun went into the fields, he cried out and wept to the merciful Heaven. Why did he cry out and weep?" Mencius said, "He was full of complaint and longing." Wan Zhang said, "'When one's parents love one, one is glad and does not forget them; when one's parents hate one, one works hard and does not complain.' Did Shun complain, then?" Mencius said, "Chang Xi asked Gongming Gao, 'As for Shun going into the fields, I have had your explanation of that; but I do not understand his crying out and weeping to the merciful Heaven and to his parents.' Gongming Gao said, 'That is something you would not understand.' Gongming Gao thought that the heart of a filial son could not be so indifferent as to say, 'I do my utmost ploughing the fields and fulfil my duty as a son, and that is all. If my parents do not love me, what is that to me?' The Emperor [Yao] sent his own children, nine sons and two daughters, along with the hundred officials, oxen and sheep, and full granaries, to serve Shun in the midst of the fields. Many of the scholars of the world went to him, and the Emperor was about to hand over the whole world to him. Yet because he was not in accord with his parents, he was like a man in utter need with nowhere to turn. To be delighted in by the scholars of the world is what men desire, yet it was not enough to relieve his sorrow. Beauty is what men desire, and he had the Emperor's two daughters as wives, yet it was not enough to relieve his sorrow. Riches are what men desire, and he had the riches of the whole world, yet it was not enough to relieve his sorrow. Honour is what men desire, and he had the honour of being Son of Heaven, yet it was not enough to relieve his sorrow. Being delighted in by others, beauty, riches and honour: none of these was enough to relieve his sorrow. Only being in accord with his parents could relieve it. When a man is young, he longs for his parents. When he comes to know the charms of beauty, he longs for young and pretty girls. When he has a wife and children, he longs for his wife and children. When he takes office, he longs for his ruler, and if he does not win his ruler's favour, he burns inside. A man of great filial piety longs for his parents all his life. In the great Shun I have seen one who still longed for them at fifty."

Wan Zhang asked, "The Ode says, 'How does one go about taking a wife? One must first tell one's parents.' If anyone should have followed these words, it was Shun. Why then did Shun marry without telling them?" Mencius said, "If he had told them, he would not have been able to marry. That a man and a woman should live together is the greatest of human relations. If he had told them, he would have had to give up the greatest of human relations, and that would have made him resent his parents. That is why he did not tell them." Wan Zhang said, "As for Shun marrying without telling them, I have had your explanation. But why did the Emperor give Shun his daughters without telling [Shun's parents]?" Mencius said, "The Emperor too knew that if he told them, he would not be able to give them in marriage." Wan Zhang said, "Shun's parents sent him to repair the granary, then took away the ladder, and Gusou set fire to the granary. They sent him to dredge the well, and when he had got out [by another way], they followed up by filling it in. Xiang said, 'The plot to bury the lord of the city was all my doing. His oxen and sheep go to my parents, his granaries go to my parents. His shield and spear are mine, his lute is mine, his carved bow is mine, and his two wives shall look after my bed.' Xiang went into Shun's house, and there was Shun on his couch playing the lute. Xiang said, 'I was thinking of you so anxiously,' and looked embarrassed. Shun said, 'Here are all my officers and people; you help me govern them.' I wonder whether Shun did not know that Xiang meant to kill him?" Mencius said, "How could he not have known? But when Xiang was sad, he was sad, and when Xiang was glad, he was glad." "Then was Shun only pretending to be glad?" Mencius said, "No. Once someone sent a live fish to Zichan of Zheng. Zichan had his pond-keeper keep it in the pond. The pond-keeper cooked it, and reported back, saying, 'When I first let it go, it was sluggish; after a little while it was swimming about freely, and then off it went.' Zichan said, 'It has found its place! It has found its place!' The pond-keeper went out and said, 'Who says Zichan is wise? I had already cooked and eaten it, and he says, "It has found its place! It has found its place!"' So a gentleman can be deceived by what seems reasonable, but it is hard to trap him with what is against the Way. Xiang came in the manner of a loving brother, so Shun sincerely believed him and was glad. What pretence was there in that?"

Wan Zhang asked, "Xiang made it his daily business to try to kill Shun. When Shun became Son of Heaven, why did he only banish him?" Mencius said, "He gave him a fief. Some say he banished him." Wan Zhang said, "Shun exiled the Minister of Works to Youzhou, banished Huandou to Mount Chong, killed [the ruler of] the Sanmiao at Sanwei, and imprisoned Gun at Mount Yu until his death. He punished these four criminals and the whole world submitted, because he had punished those who were not benevolent. Xiang was the most unbenevolent of all, yet he was given Youbi as a fief. What crime had the people of Youbi committed? Is this really how a benevolent man behaves? Others he punishes, but his brother he enfeoffs?" Mencius said, "A benevolent man does not store up anger against his brother or harbour resentment against him; he simply holds him dear and loves him. Holding him dear, he wants him to be honoured; loving him, he wants him to be rich. Giving him Youbi as a fief was to make him rich and honoured. If he himself were Son of Heaven and his brother a commoner, could he be said to hold him dear and love him?" "May I ask what is meant by those who say he banished him?" Mencius said, "Xiang was not allowed to act in his own state. The Son of Heaven sent officials to govern it and to collect its tribute and taxes [for Xiang]. That is why it was called banishment. How could Xiang have been allowed to oppress the people there? Even so, Shun wished to see him often, and so Xiang came to court again and again. 'He did not wait for the tribute season; on matters of government he received the ruler of Youbi.' This is what it means."

Xianqiu Meng asked, "There is a saying: 'A scholar of great virtue cannot be treated as a subject by his ruler or as a son by his father.' When Shun stood facing south [as sovereign], Yao led the feudal lords facing north to pay him homage, and Gusou also faced north to pay him homage. When Shun saw Gusou, his face showed unease. Confucius said, 'At that time the world was in peril; how precarious it was!' I wonder whether this saying is true?" Mencius said, "No. These are not the words of a gentleman; they are the talk of country folk from eastern Qi. When Yao was old, Shun acted as regent. The Canon of Yao says, 'After twenty-eight years, Fangxun [Yao] passed away. The people mourned as if for their own father and mother, and for three years all music of the eight kinds of instruments was silenced within the four seas.' Confucius said, 'There are not two suns in the sky, nor two kings over the people.' If Shun had already been Son of Heaven and had also led the feudal lords of the world in three years' mourning for Yao, there would have been two Sons of Heaven." Xianqiu Meng said, "As for Shun not treating Yao as a subject, I have had your explanation. But the Ode says, 'Under the whole of heaven there is no land that is not the king's; to the shores of all the land there is no one who is not the king's subject.' Once Shun had become Son of Heaven, may I ask how Gusou could not be his subject?" Mencius said, "That ode does not mean this. It is about [an officer] who toiled in the king's service and could not care for his parents. He is saying, 'All this is the king's business, yet I alone am made to toil, as if I alone were worthy.' So those who explain the Odes should not let the words distort the phrase, nor the phrase distort the meaning. To meet the poet's meaning with one's own understanding is the way to grasp it. If one went by the phrase alone, there is the ode 'The Milky Way', which says, 'Of the remaining black-haired people of Zhou, not one is left.' If one believed these words literally, there would have been no survivors in Zhou. The highest thing a filial son can do is to honour his parents, and the highest way of honouring one's parents is to support them with the whole world. To be father of the Son of Heaven is the highest honour; to be supported with the whole world is the highest support. The Ode says, 'Ever filial in his thoughts, his filial thoughts became a pattern.' This is what it means. The Book says, '[Shun] went respectfully to see Gusou, reverent and full of awe, and Gusou too became truly agreeable.' This is a case of the father being unable to treat him as a son."

Wan Zhang said, "Is it true that Yao gave the world to Shun?" Mencius said, "No. The Son of Heaven cannot give the world to anyone." "Then who gave Shun the world?" Mencius said, "Heaven gave it to him." "When Heaven gave it to him, did it command him in so many words?" Mencius said, "No. Heaven does not speak. It simply shows its will through his conduct and his affairs." "How does it show its will through his conduct and his affairs?" Mencius said, "The Son of Heaven can recommend a man to Heaven, but he cannot make Heaven give him the world. A feudal lord can recommend a man to the Son of Heaven, but he cannot make the Son of Heaven make him a feudal lord. A great officer can recommend a man to a feudal lord, but he cannot make the feudal lord make him a great officer. In the past, Yao recommended Shun to Heaven, and Heaven accepted him; he presented him to the people, and the people accepted him. That is why I say Heaven does not speak, but simply shows its will through conduct and affairs." "May I ask how he recommended him to Heaven and Heaven accepted him, and presented him to the people and the people accepted him?" Mencius said, "He had him preside over the sacrifices, and all the spirits enjoyed them: that was Heaven accepting him. He had him preside over affairs, and affairs were well ordered and the people were content with him: that was the people accepting him. Heaven gave it to him and the people gave it to him. That is why I say the Son of Heaven cannot give the world to anyone. Shun assisted Yao for twenty-eight years. That is not something a man can bring about; it was Heaven. When Yao died and the three years of mourning were over, Shun withdrew from Yao's son to the south of the Southern River. But the feudal lords of the world who came to court went not to Yao's son but to Shun; those with lawsuits went not to Yao's son but to Shun; and those who sang songs sang not of Yao's son but of Shun. That is why I say it was Heaven. Only after this did he go to the Middle Kingdom and take his seat as Son of Heaven. If he had simply moved into Yao's palace and pushed Yao's son aside, that would have been usurpation, not Heaven's gift. The Great Declaration says, 'Heaven sees as my people see; Heaven hears as my people hear.' This is what it means."

Wan Zhang asked, "People say, 'With Yu, virtue declined: he passed the throne not to the worthiest man but to his own son.' Is that so?" Mencius said, "No, it is not so. If Heaven gives it to the worthiest, it goes to the worthiest; if Heaven gives it to the son, it goes to the son. In the past, Shun recommended Yu to Heaven, and seventeen years later Shun died. When the three years of mourning were over, Yu withdrew from Shun's son to Yangcheng. The people of the world followed Yu, just as after Yao's death they had followed not Yao's son but Shun. Yu recommended Yi to Heaven, and seven years later Yu died. When the three years of mourning were over, Yi withdrew from Yu's son to the north side of Mount Ji. But those who came to court and those with lawsuits went not to Yi but to Qi, saying, 'He is our ruler's son.' Those who sang songs sang not of Yi but of Qi, saying, 'He is our ruler's son.' Danzhu [Yao's son] was unworthy, and Shun's son was unworthy as well. Shun assisted Yao and Yu assisted Shun for many years, and they bestowed their bounty on the people for a long time. Qi was worthy and able to carry on the Way of Yu with reverence. Yi assisted Yu for only a few years and had not bestowed his bounty on the people for long. That Shun, Yu and Yi differed so much in how long they served, and that their sons were worthy or unworthy, was all of Heaven, not something men can bring about. What is done though no one does it is Heaven; what comes though no one brings it is fate. For a commoner to come to possess the world, his virtue must be like that of Shun or Yu, and there must also be a Son of Heaven to recommend him. That is why Zhongni did not possess the world. When the world passes by inheritance, Heaven sets aside [an heir] only if he is like Jie or Zhou. That is why Yi, Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou did not possess the world. Yi Yin assisted Tang to become king of the world. When Tang died, Taiding had died before he could be set on the throne; Waibing reigned two years and Zhongren four. Taijia overturned the laws and statutes of Tang, and Yi Yin banished him to Tong. After three years Taijia repented of his errors, reproached himself and set himself right; at Tong he came to dwell in benevolence and move toward righteousness. After three years more of heeding Yi Yin's instruction, he returned to Bo. The Duke of Zhou's not possessing the world was like the case of Yi under Xia and Yi Yin under Yin. Confucius said, 'In Tang and Yu [Yao and Shun] the throne was handed on to the worthy; under the sovereigns of Xia, Yin and Zhou it passed by inheritance. The principle was the same.'"

Wan Zhang asked, "People say, 'Yi Yin sought Tang's favour by his skill at cutting and cooking.' Is that so?" Mencius said, "No, it is not so. Yi Yin was ploughing in the fields of Youxin, delighting in the Way of Yao and Shun. If something was not right or not according to the Way, he would not have given it a glance even if he were offered the whole world as his salary, nor looked at it even if he were offered a thousand teams of horses. If something was not right or not according to the Way, he would not give the least thing to others nor take the least thing from them. Tang sent men with gifts to invite him. Unmoved, he said, 'What do I want with Tang's gifts? Is it not better for me to stay among the fields and delight in the Way of Yao and Shun?' Only after Tang had sent three times to invite him did he change his mind completely and say, 'Rather than stay among the fields and delight in the Way of Yao and Shun by myself, is it not better to make this ruler a ruler like Yao and Shun? Is it not better to make these people a people like those of Yao and Shun? Is it not better to see it happen with my own eyes? Heaven, in giving birth to this people, has made those who first understand awaken those who understand later, and those who first awaken awaken those who awaken later. I am one of Heaven's people who has awakened first. I will awaken this people with this Way. If I do not awaken them, who will?' He thought that if any common man or woman in the world did not share in the bounty of Yao and Shun, it was as if he himself had pushed them into a ditch. So heavily did he take the burden of the world upon himself. That is why he went to Tang and urged him to attack Xia and save the people. I have never heard of anyone who bent himself and set others straight, much less one who disgraced himself and set the world straight. The sages acted differently: some kept far off and some drew near, some left and some did not leave, but it all came back to keeping themselves pure. I have heard that he sought Tang's favour by the Way of Yao and Shun; I have never heard that he did it by cutting and cooking. The Instructions of Yi say, 'Heaven's punishment began with the attack on [Jie's] palace at Mu; I began it from Bo.'"

Wan Zhang asked, "Some say that in Wey Confucius lodged with the ulcer doctor, and in Qi with the attendant Ji Huan. Is that so?" Mencius said, "No, it is not so. That was made up by busybodies. In Wey he lodged with Yan Chouyou. The wife of Mizi and the wife of Zilu were sisters. Mizi said to Zilu, 'If Confucius lodges with me, he can become a high minister of Wey.' Zilu told Confucius this. Confucius said, 'There is fate.' Confucius came forward according to the rites and withdrew according to righteousness, and whether he obtained office or not, he said, 'There is fate.' If he had lodged with the ulcer doctor or the attendant Ji Huan, that would have been to disregard both righteousness and fate. When Confucius was not pleased with Lu and Wey, and Huan, the Master of the Horse in Song, was about to waylay and kill him, he passed through Song in disguise. At that time, though he was in difficulty, he lodged with Zhenzi, the Master of the City Walls, who was a minister of Zhou, Marquis of Chen. I have heard that you judge ministers at court by the guests they receive, and ministers from abroad by the hosts they lodge with. If Confucius had lodged with the ulcer doctor or the attendant Ji Huan, how could he have been Confucius?"

Wan Zhang asked, "Some say, 'Baili Xi sold himself to a cattle-keeper of Qin for five sheepskins and fed cattle, in order to seek the favour of Duke Mu of Qin.' Is that true?" Mencius said, "No, it is not so. That was made up by busybodies. Baili Xi was a man of Yu. The people of Jin offered the jade disc of Chuiji and the team of horses bred in Qu to borrow passage through Yu in order to attack Guo. Gong Zhiqi remonstrated [against allowing it], but Baili Xi did not. He knew that the Duke of Yu could not be persuaded by remonstrance, so he left and went to Qin. He was already seventy years old. If he did not know that seeking Duke Mu's favour by feeding cattle was a disgrace, could he be called wise? But knowing remonstrance would be useless and so not remonstrating, could he be called unwise? Knowing that the Duke of Yu was about to perish and leaving him beforehand, he cannot be called unwise. Being raised up in Qin at that time, he knew that Duke Mu was one with whom he could accomplish something, and so he served as his minister: could he be called unwise? As minister of Qin he made his ruler illustrious throughout the world, worthy to be handed down to later ages: could he have done that if he were not a worthy man? To sell oneself in order to make one's ruler successful is something even a villager who cares for his good name would not do. Are we to say a worthy man would do it?"
